Traditionally, in the Christian world we give the name Old Testament to the thirty-nine canonical writings that have been bequeathed to us 
the sacred traditions of Israel as a testimony of their faith in revelation 
divine. They all saw the light before the birth of our Lord 
Jesus Christ and constitute the Holy Scriptures of Judaism, to which this 
designates with the name of Tanakh, an artificial word in the Hebrew language that includes 
the three great sections called by the Jewish teachers Torah (the Law), 
Nebiim (Prophets) and Ketubim (Writings), respectively. Although in its immense 
Most were written in the Hebrew language, the lingua sacra of Israel, some 
of them (books of Ezra and Daniel) present entire chapters written in 
Aramaic, the language that the Jews adopted as a vehicle of communication 
own since the Babylonian captivity (between 586 -537 BC). The 
Aramaic is also present in other Old Testament books, although in 
smaller proportion: some verse, some specific word, or in or cases 
coloring the Hebrew text with a style that clearly shows a 
late final writing (Jeremiah, Genesis, Ecclesiastes...). 
The great group that we call the Old Testament comes to tell us  
From its first chapters to the last, an extraordinary story 
Salutis (Salvation History) which begins with the creation of the world and 
concludes with the hopeful oracles of the prophet Malachi;  a story 
whose protagonist is God, the liberating God who approaches Israel to 
rescue him from Egyptian captivity at the hands of Moses and enter into an alliance with 
him, according to the promises made to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the patriarchs 
ancestors of the Jews. As time passes and the people of 
Israel settles in the land of Canaan (the promised land), God addresses him by 
through the prophets, charismatic figures specially raised to 
correct abuses and straighten the paths of a nation always ungrateful, always 
rebellious to his divine Benefactor. Hence in the chapters and verses of 
Old Testament we find, intermingled with the most extraordinary 
promises, the most devastating judgments, and with the most terrible punishments, the 
tenderest declarations of love and mercy. 

2

Careful and careful compilation, with enormous literary quality, of 
ancient traditions and more recent oracles, from chronicles with a historical flavor 
and fictionalized narratives, of sublime epic and lyrical poetry, in addition to 
extraordinary mythical-didactic stories, the canonical Old Testament 
knows its definitive edition-compilation between the 5th and 2nd centuries BC. C. and supposes a 
titanic effort to understand God on the part of the teachers and wise men of 
the lineage of Jacob, from the not always clear tones with which it appears drawn 
the primeval Divinity of the pristine twelve tribes descended from Abraham, 
not always easily discernible from the Canaanite deities (the stigmatized 
baals of the strictest Yahwism), to the Merciful Lord who acts as 
Israel head of the nations, in order to bless the great family through him 
human. 
And most important of all: the Old Testament macro-ensemble, 
always tinged with promises of restoration, leaves open a door of 
hope for the rebellious people that is Israel and for all the peoples of the 
earth: someone who will come in the future to implant in this world the 
Kingdom of God, where there will be no more injustice or more pain. 
In this way, we Christians find in the sacred oracles 
Old Testament, distributed in four sections (Pentateuch, books 
historical, poetic-wisdom literature and prophetic books), an anticipation 
as in shadows, not totally clear, but absolutely sure, of the 
messianic times, in which the redemption of the human race must be 
definitive through the person and work of Jesus Christ.

content:
The name Pentateuch, a Greek word that means “five cases to store papyrus or parchment”, is given to the set of five 
books that the Jews designate as the Holy Torah, the Law of Moses. 
They are the following: Genesis (Gen.), Exodus (Ex.), Leviticus (Lev.), Numbers 
(Nm.) and Deuteronomy (Dt.). It contains, in fact, the Pentateuch, 
in addition to important and striking stories, the total of six hundred and thirteen 
commandments or provisions of the sacred law of Judaism, which cover the 
Decalogue or Ten Commandments (Ex. 20:1-17; Deut. 5:1-21), the so-called Code of 
the Covenant (Ex. 20:22 – 23:33), the Cultual or Ritual Decalogue (Ex. 34:14-26), the Law 
of Holiness (Lev. 17 -26) and the Deuteronomistic Code (Dt. 12-26), among others 
provisions. 
 Traditionally attributed to Moses, the liberator and great legislator 
of Israel, which would have lived around the 15th or 13th centuries BC. C., the Pentateuch 
It appears to be a masterful late compilation, from around the 5th-3rd centuries BC. C., of 
a series of traditions, sometimes very ancient, about the origins of the people of 
Israel in Egypt and in the Sinai Desert, as well as of its special election 
divine, to which are added much later provisions and stories about 
various matters. Some Jewish traditions collected in the Talmud point to 
the so-called “Great Synagogue”, presided over by the priest and scribe Ezra, 
as the cradle of the Pentateuch as we know it today. The truth is that the 
great abundance of materials of which it consists speaks clearly of a multiple 
and varied composition and writing, after a long process of selection and 
compilation that must have been carried out for almost a millennium. Since the century 
XIX, what is known as the “Hypothesis” has been spreading among scholars. 
Documentary” or Graf-Wellhausen Hypothesis (by the names of its 
first supporters), which points out four basic documents underlying the 
current redaction of the Pentateuch: a J document (Yahwist, from the divine name 
Yahweh, Jahweh in German), an E document (Elohist, from the divine name 
Elohim), a P document (Priesterschrift, in German) and a 
D (Deuteronomist), which would date as a whole from the 9th - 5th centuries BC. C. grosso 
way, with J being the oldest, coming from the historical kingdom of Judah, and P being the oldest. 
recent, from the time of the exile in Babylon and the restoration, although it echoes 
of sometimes much older rituals. Although these are classic postulates of 
Biblical studies have been considered in some circles practically up to 
our days as an irrefutable truth, the truth is that today research 
rather he opts to indicate in the origins of the Pentateuch a series of 
traditions (rather than literary documents per se), originating in

priestly origin, coming from levitical circles linked 
especially with the temple in Jerusalem. 
 Be that as it may, the imprint left on the traditions is undeniable.

Indeed, in its current arrangement, the book of Genesis tells us the

 Its first eleven chapters, to which the technical names of 
“Primitive History” or “Stories of the Origins” contain narratives of

 The narratives that follow (chap. 12 -50) collect very ancient traditions

The environmental and cultural distance with our days becomes more evident.  
The story of Joseph, which covers the last chapters of this second

In this way, placed by order of the scribes who wrote the

The book of Exodus compiles the most outstanding traditions regarding the

Finally, at Sinai, God shows himself in all his glory to a people

Chapters 2 0-40, except the account of Moses and the elders of Israel

Leviticus is an adjective that refers to the tribe of Levi, the tribe

 In addition, Numbers presents valuable information about

 All this amalgamation of cultic considerations and narrative stories,

 In its present form, Deuteronomy is presented as a collection of

western part of the vast Persian Empire, by its ancient inhabitants, as well as the 
reconstruction of its ruined cities, including Jerusalem itself, and above all 
all the sacred temple of Solomon. The chap. 2 shows an exhaustive list of 
those who accompanied Zerubbabel from Babylon to Judea, which precedes 
a narrative in which we read about the difficulties encountered by the newly 
arrived in their ancestral land: the hostility of the country's inhabitants, 
foreigners installed after deportation, generates large 
complications, and even a total paralysis of reconstruction work 
of Jerusalem and the temple. 
 The figure of the priest Ezra does not appear until chapter. 7, when 
presents in Jerusalem recently arrived from Babylon with a clear purpose of 
support the restoration and instruct the Jewish people in the faith and practices 
pious practices of their ancestors, very neglected at the time, or even forgotten. The 
Measures taken by Ezra imply a return to the pristine arrangements 
of the law of Moses for ancient Israel, which entails a clear confession 
of sins before God for all the impieties and iniquities committed throughout 
throughout history. The chap. 9 contains the prayer of confession pronounced by 
Ezra, to which all the people and their leaders adhere. 

36

The restoration of the people leads, in the mentality of Ezra and his 
companions, a vital need for national purity understood from the 
point of view of the Jewish ethnic group itself: marriages are dissolved by decree 
mixed and foreign and pagan women are expelled from Judea together 
with his children. The text makes it clear that there were many Jews 
who had mixed with foreign women. This radical reform is carried out 
carried out unceremoniously, so that it leaves the modern reader with a bad taste of 
mouth. It is evident that, with the works of the Chronicler, the foundations of 
an exclusivist Judaism diametrically opposed to the divine will, although 
put on piety, and against whom Jesus will launch harsh accusations in his 
moment.

Also called in other times "book 2 or 3 Esdras", according to what 
that we explained in the previous chapter, the book of Nehemiah comes 
to tell us the continuation of what we have read in the book of  
Ezra on the restoration of Jerusalem in a devastated Judea and 
full of enemies, and thus puts an end to the literary ensemble that 
known as El Cronista, allowing us to contemplate the beginnings of a 
very peculiar religious stage, which in New Testament times was 
will be called Pharisaism, and which is firmly established in the Jewish remnant recently 
settled in the land of his ancestors. 
But who really is Nehemiah? Chapter 1 shows it as a 
high official of the Persian court who has royal favor, which allows him 
move as governor to an unprotected Jerusalem where 
There are a number of Jewish families living in fear and defenseless against the 
hostility of its foreign adversaries. Nehemiah is neither a Levite nor a priest, 
but he shows a great zeal for the name of God that makes him fight in all 
the possible fronts while the city walls are rebuilt and new 
Jewish families settle there. Hence I do not just repeat the list of those who 
They came to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel that we read in the book of Ezra (ch. 7), 
but offer a new list of the inhabitants of the city (ch. 11) and another 
of the priests and Levites (chap. 12), all in the midst of joy for the 
wall dedication; Jerusalem is already protected from external attacks.  
Concerned about the material and spiritual well-being of his people, 
Nehemiah dictates laws abolishing usury (ch. 5), as well as other measures 
drastic measures aimed at strict observance of the law of Moses 
(ch. 13) . Hence, throughout the entire book, Nehemiah implores the favor 
divine for himself, because he believes he has acted correctly. 
The most important episode of the book, however, is not 
protagonist to Nehemiah himself, but to the scribe and priest Ezra, and it is that 
in which the latter, on the occasion of a solemn festival, and in a climate of 
exultation over the restoration of Israel, reads to the people the book of the Law of 
Moses (an excerpt or summary of the content of our current Pentate uco, which 
more probably) and explains it with the help of the Levites (chap. 8), having done 
which a long confession of sins is pronounced (ch. 9) and the people 
commits to keep the covenant of Moses, which again becomes the 
people of God (ch. 10): Judaism was born as a religious system and 
distinctive of a human community that seemed doomed to extinction. 

38

The book of Nehemiah is not difficult to understand for the reader of 
our days, but, as with Ezra's, it does not leave a taste 
nice. Even understanding their peculiar circumstances and their vital environment, 
Whoever reads the book of Nehemiah today does not fail to observe a rigorism and even 
a cruelty that seems unnecessary. 
Be that as it may, this writing completes well the historical cycle of the Chronicler and 
comes to convey the idea that God never leaves aside his people, nor 
even in the midst of the greatest tribulations.

Cataloged by many scholars as a Jewish didactic novel of 
late period, the book of Esther presents a double role: the 
young Jewish woman of this name who becomes queen of the Persian Empire, and 
his relative and mentor Mard Ochei, of the lineage of King Saul (2:5), with 
a clear antagonist: the evil Haman, who is supposed to be the offspring of 
a cursed race (3:1), staunch enemy of the Jews and unfortunate 
ancestor of all the anti-Semites who have splashed Israelite blood on the 
pages of human history. 
 The fact that God's name is not mentioned even once in 
the entire story, and that the work seems written solely to justify a 
holiday, Purim, which is not part of Israel's religious calendar 
based on the law of Moses, it generated quite a few problems for the teachers 
Jews when introducing the book of Esther into the sacred canon. In fact, no 
entered only after long discussions and thanks to the passionate argumentation at his 
favor performed by the famous Rabbi Akivá at the beginning of the Christian Era. By 
On the other hand, the Alexandrian Jews of the centuries before the birth of Christ, 
in order to give the work a clear religious meaning that they could not find anywhere. 
part, they added the apocryphal chapters that today make up the so-called Esther 
Greek and found in the Septuagint and in the Catholic versions or 
interdenominational scriptures. 
 But this does not mean that the original Hebrew work is meaningless.  
own religious While it cannot be understood as a confession of faith, 4:13-16 
gives a glimpse of a divine Providence that acts behind the scenes and everything 
directs, although in a manner incomprehensible to man, with a view to the good of 
his town. This means, in addition to the lack of supernatural manifestations, 
a thought that has evolved and has allowed a theology quite 
developed. Only then does the narrative make sense: a young Jewish woman who lives in the 
diaspora and represents the Jews who never returned to their homeland after the 
edict of Cyrus, becomes queen of the all-powerful Persian Empire and dismantles with 
his intercession the intrigues of evil Haman, so that the Jews execute 
massive revenge from his mortal enemies, and Mordecai himself 
He reaches a prominent place in the administration of the vast empire.  we can 
suppose that the author of the book of Esther, whoever he was, intended 
refute the idea that those who decided to settle in the lands of the 
deportation were impious people or disobedient to divine designs; also 
Jews located outside Judea are pious, faithful, maintain religious practices 

40

rituals such as fasting and intercession, and appear blessed by that God who 
It is never named, but it is always there. 
 The modern reader of the book of Esther will undoubtedly enjoy the features 
fictional aspects of the story, although it will not share an outcome so bloody and so 
full of the spirit of revenge, so in contrast to the broad-mindedness of the 
gospel of Christ. But this in no way diminishes the literary quality and the value of its 
fundamental message, which is none other than a Providence that always guides the 
human events with a clear purpose: blessing.

content:
Included in this special section of the Old Testament are a series 
of works of extremely high literary value, which at the same time expose the 
first fruits of the wisdom of Israel: the book of Job (Job or Jb.), the Psalms 
(Ps.), the Proverbs (Pr.), the Ecclesiastes (Ec. or Ecl.) and the Song of the 
Songs (Song), all of them late compositions, from the time of the 
restoration after the Babylonian captivity, although they seem to preserve in 
material occasions of great antiquity, or refer to traditions that could 
get lost in the night of time. Although the language in which they are written is 
is Hebrew, sometimes with obvious—and deliberate, according to 
specialists—archaisms (as in Job and in some Psalms, above all), it becomes 
It is clear that it is a somewhat Aramaicized Hebrew and sometimes with 
certain foreign vocabulary from more recent times, as is the particular case 
of Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs; something similar is found in certain 
parts of the book of Proverbs. 
 Except for a few chapters of the book of Job and the whole of the 
Ecclesiastes, these are works composed in poetic style, as intended 
reflect the Bible editions of our day in the way they are printed. but 
our Western concepts of “poetry” or “poem” do not correspond n 
exactly what was meant by such is among the ancient Israelites: not 
rhyme does not exist, nor does the type of compositions to which we are accustomed 
in the West (tercets, quartets, serventesios, octosyllabic verses, etc.). to a 
Thus, the current reader who approaches the Scriptures in translations can grasp 
something of Hebrew poetic art, for example, in the parallelisms of ideas or 
words, or in the division of the verses into hemistics that each contain 
a fundamental idea.  To tell the truth, it is not uncomfortable or unpleasant 
Hebrew poetry to Western ears; It is simply another way of 
poetic expression. 
 This wisdom literature, as its name indicates, wants to reflect and 
transmit the wisdom of Israel at a time when the Jewish people live the 
crisis of a return to the homeland and a settlement in Judea in the middle of 
strong opposition, if not outright hostility (cf. the books of Ezra and 
Nehemiah). The Jews returning from Babylon, especially their elites 
intellectuals, have lived in captivity with realities very different from those 
that until then they had known, cultures with very ancient roots that 
They have their own conception of the world, of man and of the gods, and that 
They express through mythical language and elaborate literature their  

42

peculiar worldview. Hence the Jewish sages wish, not only to respond, 
but also emulate that intellectual activity, sometimes using a language 
mythical taken from various sources, but starting from a different concept of the 
reality. The God revealed to the patriarchs and Moses is the only God, and also 
the Creator of all that exists. Unlike the Mesopotamian cultures, 
who made their gods a transcript of their human world, and life a 
shadowy existence from which the powerful briefly escaped, wisdom 
of Israel will start from the opposite idea: man is the image of God (cf. 
called “First account of Creation” in Gen. 1:1 – 2:4a, true 
monument of Hebrew wisdom) and therefore must act according to its 
elevated dignity as such, making the world and life a praise 
perpetuates the Creator. This is the reason why the wisdom of Israel does not seek 
mere speculation about the cosmos or being, as the 
first Greek philosophy, but that it focuses on man and his needs, on 
relationships between human beings, because the great principle that defines it is 
the fear of YHWH (Prov. 1:7a). This is the only way to explain that these books, some of them 
which were criticized and discussed by the rabbis, so that they did not want 
include them in the sacred canon, have reached us and continue 
offering us the freshness and grace they had when they were written.

This unique writing receives its title from the name of its 
human protagonist, an opulent oriental patriarch of the most 
remote antiquity, which does not belong to the lineage of Israel (1:1), but is, 
Nevertheless, a fearer of God and a pious man among the pious, 
so much so that in popular terminology it has become 
paradigm of patience (James 5:11). The plot, very simple, comes to pose the 
problem of the pain of the innocent, the eternal theme of the just sufferer, of the 
which the wise men of the Mesopotamian Fertile Crescent already echo (poem 
Akkadian Ludlul Bel Nemeqi), and captures it through a story very well 
constructed, in which current exegetes see several sources: first, 
two initial chapters in prose, which narrate the challenge launched by 
Satan to God about Job's integrity, thereby subjecting him to 
very harsh trials and losses, and a final chapter, chapter 42, also in prose, in 
which recounts the restoration of the patriarch to his pristine greatness. And in the middle, 
chapters 3 -41, in verse, of which 3 -31 present the diatribes between a 
Job troubled and full of misfortunes, and three friends who accuse him of suffering what 
deserves for his injustice, while he maintains his integrity and denounces the 
injustice of God towards his person; 32 -37 introduce the character of Elihu, 
impetuous and zealous young man who attacks Job with real viciousness 
vindicating the justice of God; and 38-41, in which God himself intervenes. 
 Who or who were the authors of such a magnificent staging? 
Ancient Jewish traditions point to several possibilities, dating back to Job himself 
until Moses, but they do not resist critical analysis, which shows a composition 
late, from the time of the restoration after the Babylonian captivity, and from 
multiple hands. Most specialists agree that, although 
The prose and verse texts constitute different compositions, a masterful 
editor made them agree on a well-orchestrated plot, although the chapters 
referring to Elihu (32-37) have all the signs of a later addition to  
involve a Jew in the plot. 
 The modern reader understands the story of Job with relative ease. Even 
the poetic parts in which accusations and defenses, give and take, are read, 
Despite their archaic style, they are accessible to the understanding of today's man. Of 
special way, God's intervention in chapters. 38 -41 coat shades 
sublime, with images of unusual beauty about the natural world, 
expressed in accordance with the knowledge of the time, without disdaining the figures of 

44

mythical beings (behemoth and leviathan), which makes this part in particular, and even 
of the book as a whole, a work of the first magnitude in universal literature. 
 But the author (or definitive editor) of the book of Job can not only 
classify yourself as a writer, a poet or a wise man. He is also a great theologian. 
The great challenge posed at the beginning of the plot about Job's integrity, if 
Job serves God without expecting anything in return, he finds a positive response. In 
In the midst of suffering and humiliation, the patriarch takes refuge in divine justice, 
albeit in sometimes challenging tones that, in the end, provoke his regret. 
God does not give an answer to the reason for human suffering; is limited to 
unfold before the eyes of Job (and the current reader) a creation beyond 
beautiful, in which not all beings are useful or generate real benefit to the 
man, but they do appear beautiful, and contribute to the glory of the Creator. Of 
In fact, God shows his displeasure with Job's friends and their religiosity 
utilitarian, the do ut des that has always had, and has, so many supporters. 
 In this way, the book of Job becomes a hymn to the Creator God, 
at the same time as a hymn to the purest, simplest religiosity, that 
that is paid to the Supreme Maker simply because he is one.

For many, it is the book of Psalms, not only the most beautiful writing. 
and most sublime of the Bible, but the paradigm of all literature 
scriptural poetics. Considered by specialists as a work 
summit of Hebrew and Eastern poetics, more than two millennia ago 
contributes to liturgical praise to the God of Israel and Father of our 
Lord Jesus Christ, both in the rites of the synagogue and in those of the Church 
universal. 
 Its one hundred and fifty compositions appear distributed in the 
present in five books, like a Torah or poetic Pentateuch, according to some 
specialists, although, according to the editions of the sacred text, certain psalms 
They can have one number or another, and even the count of their verses 
may vary. All this shows that it is not an easy task to always delimit your 
content or the limits of their compositions. Although a very old tradition 
wanted to attribute the whole set to King David, the great singer of Israel, today 
Various sources are indicated, that is, several authors (and not always identifiable) 
in its composition. In fact, the headings of many psalms—which in 
some current editions of the Bible count as the text of each 
song, but not in all of them - they do not indicate that David was its author, but other 
different characters (Asaf, the sons of Korah, Moses himself, Nathan the Ezrahite, 
etc.). It is not really easy to discern the authorship of the one hundred and fifty psalms as such. 
as we read them today: on the one hand, the headings reflect periods 
after its final writing, and obey certain Jewish traditions 
more than a serious study carried out on the compositions themselves; and for him 
On the other hand, the texts themselves resist a simple pigeonholing of the songs. 
in relation to specific characters or periods. Nobody doubts 
currently that some psalms, or certain parts of them at least, can 
go back, in fact, to the time of David, but the whole shows a 
definitive composition and a rather late compilation of the Psalter, of the 
restoration after the Babylonian captivity, and certainly of the Levitical circles 
linked to the temple of Jerusalem and the reestablishment of the cultic liturgy. 
 The psalms have very varied themes. Among them we find 
compositions that seem to respond to very individual situations of 
each psalmist, like the famous Psalm 23 or Shepherd's Psalm, or Psalm 51, 
also designated as the Miserere from Latin translations, both 
traditionally attributed to David. Some psalms have a clear flavor of 
liturgical confession of the faith of Israel, such as 105, a summary of the History of 

46

the Salvation that would point to the Levitical schools. Psalm 137, for its part, 
attributed to the captives in Babylon, exudes true hatred and desire for 
revenge against Israel's oppressors. The 90, however, attributed to Moses, and 
91, called in the Protestant tradition Luther's Psalm, given the appreciation that 
The great Reformer felt for him, they are songs of trust in God. 119 is 
a masterful composition of sapiential tones that exalts the value of the law 
divine. Without forgetting the so-called Messianic Psalms, in which tradition 
Christian has seen prophetic anticipations of the life and ministry of Jesus (2, 
22, 110, among others). 
 It is understandable, then, that the Psalter is the favorite book of many faithful.  
Christians of our days and may they find in him inspiration and a guide for their 
spirituality. But we cannot ignore that they are also found in the Psalms.  
abundant samples of a somewhat archaic, even primitive, religiosity, 
diametrically opposed to the gospel. Perhaps this dichotomy is the reason for the 
preference for the Psalms of so many current readers of the Scriptures. Of 
Somehow, these masterful one hundred and fifty songs are echoed by all 
the ups and downs, experiences, joys and disappointments of human life, even more so, of 
believers' own existential experience of faith.

Under the name of the Book of Proverbs - in Hebrew Mishlé 
Shelomoh, “comparisons of Solomon”—we find a beautiful 
collection of sentences and sayings of various types, product of the 
wisdom of Israel, and attributed to King Solomon, son of David (1:1), the 
quintessential wise man of Hebrew traditions (1 Kings 4:30-34). He 
The same book recognizes the proverbs as specifically Solomonic. 
included in chapters 10-29, alluding, as if in passing, to a 
wisdom school from the time of King Hezekiah (25:1), which would have compiled them  
and classified. Regarding the authorship of the rest, only the proverbs of the chapters 
30 and 31 seem to be able to be attributed to specific characters: a certain Agur, son of 
Jaque, and a king Lemuel, respectively, who are not entirely 
unknown, but who would not exactly be called Jews, but rather 
oriental. All of this points to a definitive writing of the book in the epochs 
recent, undoubtedly from the restoration, and as a product of the renovation 
nationality of the people after the Babylonian captivity. 
 Proverbs is a pleasant book for the current reader of the Holy Bible, 
given his brief and comparative style of sentence, at least in a good part 
of its constituent materials. But even in the opening chapters, where 
we find more developed examples and discourses, we find a style 
close, warm and paternalistic, which is close to us. The society that 
describes this book as a whole is not the one we find in the first 
historical books of the Old Testament, mainly rural and 
agriculture, subsistence in the middle of a country inhabited by natives 
pagans who had to be fought. The vital medium of the book of Proverbs 
It is rather an urban type society in which even women are seen 
widely revalued as a person capable of making decisions and carrying out 
term own initiatives (chap. 31). More than one specialist has said, and with 
reason, that in its chapters and verses we basically hear the voice of the 
Jewish teachers who specifically instruct the younger ones in good 
families (hierosolimitan aristocracy of the 5th and 4th centuries BC?) through 
simplified examples and stories, in which the teacher speaks like a father to 
his children; In fact, the teacher is conceived as a father to his disciples, 
those that form with love.  
This capital work of Jewish thought develops before our eyes the 
basic principle of true wisdom, that which makes Israel a people 
different from those around them, and that it is nothing but the fear of YHWH (1:7), true 

48

universal that comes to Christianity as a fundamental principle. Likewise, 
offers an image of this wisdom as a personification, not a mere 
abstract concept, so that it acts like a teacher who invites the 
men to instruction and knowledge embodied in a righteous life (ch. 
9). Furthermore, the wise men of Israel come to conceive this wisdom as a 
kind of divine hypostasis and privileged witness of the birth of our 
world by the work of the Creator (8:22-31), in which some Fathers of the Church 
ancients saw a prefiguration of Christ. 
Hence the perennial value of this book, its universal principles and 
its great literary beauty, which make it an authentic masterpiece whose 
reading continues to be enriching and formative for Jewish believers and 
Christians.

The name Ecclesiastes, of clear Greek origin, is the translation offered by the 
Septuagint from the Hebrew word qohélet, “preacher”, “one who speaks 
before the popular assembly”, and refers to the alleged author of the book or 
narrator of its content, who presents himself as son of David and king 
in Jerusalem (1:1). Hence certain Jewish traditions have identified it without 
more like Solomon and have tried to find in the twelve chapters that 
This work is made up of clear allusions to the reign of the illustrious monarch. But one 
simple superficial reading of the book of Ecclesiastes is more than enough to 
verify that this tradition—albeit late—lacks any real foundation. The 
Solomonic authorship is nothing other than a literary fiction and very little 
suitable, by the way, to praise the Davidic monarchy, since the book of the 
Ecclesiastes comes to describe a type of society and certain conditions 
economic, political and even moral, which would leave the 
exalted son of David and his government, relegating them to the realm of fable 
how much we read about him in 1 Kings or 2 Chronicles. Both this data and the 
style of writing and its vocabulary, point rather to the time of the 
Jewish restoration under Persian rule as the moment in which it saw the light. Your 
author, as happens in so many cases, is unknown to us, but 
We deduce that he is a profound thinker, a true master of 
Israel restored by Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah. A true wise man.  
The book of Ecclesiastes is not difficult for us to read, but 
surprising for its negative, bitter, almost depressing taste at times, so 
as well as for its crude realism and its materialism so far from the ideals 
evangelicals, which points to a background of serious crisis, typical of the second period 
turbulent histories and profound identity losses.  Everything you have 
place under heaven is nothing but pure vanity of vanities (1:2) and human life, 
which would seem to be meaningless and have no continuity after the 
death, is reduced to a mere enjoyment of the immediate earthly (chap. 9). But at  
At the same time, the author offers us wise reflections on the value of time 
(3:1-8), and never closes the door to the presence of God in the lives of men. 
On the contrary, God—who is never mentioned by the Sacred Tetragrammaton 
YHWH—is always sovereign, and the one to whom we must render an account of 
our actions (chap. 12) . Finally, although man may be ungrateful and 
unfair to his Creator, God does everything well and has given the species 
human the gift of intuiting eternity (3:11). 

50

It is nothing strange, therefore, that the 
book of Ecclesiastes as the exponent, perhaps, of a Jewish philosophical school 
contemporary of classical Greek philosophy, which would have given rise to the 
thought of the Sadducees of Jesus' time. Without reaching an affirmation 
so resounding, we can indicate that the book of Ecclesiastes represents the point 
from the point of view of those who, faced with the realities of a world that does not know 
complete the patterns that shaped the birth of Israel at the time, 
They are going to vindicate the permanent values of the Jewish religion by giving them a 
varnish in keeping with the new times, without explicit mentions of situations or 
characters of the History of Salvation, but making the only God a 
ultimate reality capable of coloring and fully justifying everything that 
seems dark or vain in human existence.

Although also attributed to Solomon (1:1), and for the same reasons 
than other exponents of wisdom literature previously reviewed, the 
book to which we give, according to its Hebrew designation, the name of 
Song of Songs—that is, the most excellent song—is presented in a 
completely different way from the rest of the wisdom books of the Old Testament. It is not only a poetic work, just like Proverbs, Psalms, 
or Job, but appears evidently composed as a dramatization. In 
This sense would be, mutatis mutandis, as some commentators have pointed out, 
the only play that contains the Bible. 
 Just as a few other Old Testament books (Esther, 
Ecclesiastes, Ezekiel), the Song of Songs had trouble entering into 
the Hebrew canon of the Holy Scriptures. The fact that God does not appear in 
the entire plot, as well as the high erotic tone of the narration, sometimes with 
very explicit images, generated great scruples in some teachers 
Jews, who saw in this work a mere worldly and even immoral piece. One 
Once again, it was the passionate apology of the famous Rabbi Akiv that convinced 
who doubted, so in the end they made the final decision to 
include it in the canon. 
 The Song of Songs presents the relationship between a man and a woman. 
young women who, it seems, have difficulties finding themselves 
and fully enjoy your loving intimacy. There are many obstacles 
that come between them, but love is always more powerful and always 
triumphs. The mention of Solomon (3:6-11) and the existence of responding choirs 
to the plants of the young lovers (1:8; 6:1; 8:5,8-9) raise difficulties for the 
time to distribute the text among the acts before. In fact, not all scholars 
They agree when deducing how many there really are: two (the 
beloved, who would be King Solomon in his youth, and the beloved, a young woman 
Shulamite) or three (the beloved, the beloved and Solomon, who would be the antagonist, 
pretend to the Shulamite woman engaged to her beloved, a young peasant). 
Likewise, the big question also arises about the interpretation of the 
narrated story: is it a real event that occurred in the times of Solomon and 
presented as a poetic dramatization, or is it, perchance, a simple fiction 
literary? And above all, what is its spiritual value, which justifies the 
inclusion of the Song of Songs in the sacred canon? To this last 
question has been answered in various ways: some Jewish rabbis have 
wanted to see in the beloved God himself and Isra, captive this 

52

last in Babylon, represented by Solomon and his palace splendor. Since 
the first centuries of Christianity, the Fathers have seen in the beloved and the 
loved the figures of Christ and the Church. 
 Be that as it may, the Song of Songs is presented today to the reader of the 
Holy Scriptures as a piece of clear late composition due to its level of 
language and its style, at the same time as a masterpiece of literature 
universal. It very well deserves its place within the Holy Bible for exalting the 
love between two human beings in all its greatness, which is the best reflection of 
great love of God for all men and for his people.

content:
They constitute the last major section of the Christian Old Testament, 
and they receive this name because they are traditionally works 
attributed to great prophets of Israel, the so-called “prophets 
authors”, although current criticism has largely qualified these 
attributions by pointing out that these books that now bear names of 
prophets appear to be works of a school rather than of an individual author, as 
becomes evident in some very specific cases. In general terms, the so-called 
Prophetic Books coincide with the section of the Hebrew Bible designated as 
Nebiim, more specifically the Nebiim acharonim or “later prophets.” so 
They only differ in the fact that the Christian distribution of the Old Testament admits among the prophetic books the Lamentations (attributed to the 
prophet Jeremiah) and the book of Daniel, two works that the Hebrew Bible relegates to its 
third great section, the Ketubim or Writings. 
 Traditionally, the Prophetic Books have been classified into two large 
sets: the so-called Major Prophets and the Minor Prophets, the latter

so that it does not contain any accusation against his own compatriots. No 
We read in his brief writing no mention of what other prophets of the time 
say about the injustice or idolatry of the Hebrews, and there is not the briefest 
allusion to the destruction of Judah and Jerusalem being due to a punishment 
divine. Obadiah feels compassion for his defeated people and the conditions 
of danger and humiliation to which an opportunistic and inhuman Edom has 
subjected, ignoring any kinship or neighborhood. The 
Final verses speak of the restoration of Israel as a fact in the 
divine purpose, and draw a picture of glory and prosperity of the people 
rehabilitated, but without room for ambiguity: “the kingdom will be YHWH's”, it is read in the 
last words of v. 21. In this way, the prophet makes it clear that Judah and 
Israel are only beneficiaries of divine goodness, never protagonists 
principals of the saving drama. 

72

For the modern reader of the Holy Bible, the language of Obadiah can 
It may seem a bit strange, but it conveys well the compassion and mercy of 
God for a disadvantaged nation and prey to the strongest in the world. 
moment. In this sense, its theological relevance is undeniable.

Although it is traditionally included among the prophetic books, the 
The book of Jonah should be better classified among the writings 
narratives of the Old Testament, not only because of their style, but 
also for its content. In fact, the figure of Jonah who 
appears in its four chapters has become one of the 
universal references of biblical literature, due to the event of the great fish that 
relates (1:17 – 2:10 or 2:1-11, depending on the editions), used by Jesus himself 
to illustrate his resurrection (Mt. 12:39-40), and which has been represented by the 
artists from all periods of the Christian Era. 
 In fact, except for the song or psalm of chap. 2, poetic piece of great 
quality clearly inserted later, the book of Jonah shows all 
the features of the didactic novel after the Babylonian captivity (cf. the book 
of Ruth), and constitutes, without a doubt, a writing of firm protest against the 
fundamentalist and inhuman reforms of Ezra and Nehemiah to safeguard the 
racial and religious purity of the Jews. The message of the book of Jonah is very 
simple: God has my mercy on all sinful human beings, even 
of the vilest pagans, since they do not know how to distinguish between their right hand and their 
left hand, and extends his compassion and kindness to the animals (4:11). 
To convey it he uses a figure from times past, the historical prophet  
Jonah son of Amittai, who had lived around the 8th century BC. C. in Israel 
northern and in the reign of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25), presenting him as 
protagonist of a bizarre story, very difficult to verify in the 
real world, and in which the main tones are of permanent flight and 
desperate of God, in order not to fulfill a very precise task, for 
know in advance that he is doomed to failure: God is too 
merciful to want the destruction of anyone, not even enemies 
of his people, although he announces it with all possible rigor (chap. 3). All of this 
makes its author, unknown to us, not only a great master of 
Hebrew language, whose ancient style it imitates very well from the beginning of the 
first verse, but, and above all, a great theologian, a thinker who 
knows how to capture the true essence of the God of Israel in the face of Jewish exclusivism, 
that pathetic fundamentalism and irreverent tones so well represented in the 
figure of Jonah himself (ch. 4). 
 The book of Jonah, in short, is easy and enjoyable to read, almost 
fun, for our contemporaries, not only for its stylistic features 
alive and captivating, but for the core of its message, so close to the New 

74

Testament, to the atmosphere of the gospel. For this reason it is considered 
unanimously considered one of the great achievements of literature 
Old Testament, as well as a worthy representative of its theological standards 
higher.

With the prophecy of Micah of Moreset we once again immerse ourselves 
once again in the atmosphere of the decadent kingdoms of Judah and Israel, 
just as they were in the 8th century BC. C., time of deceptive prosperity 
that poorly hid the imminent catastrophe, although the people of God 
was unable to see it. Micah is a contemporary of others 
prophets, such as the Ephraimite Hosea and the Judaites Amos and Isaiah, the essentials of 
whose messages he shares, first because the situation that is presented to his 
eyes is identical, and second, because it is the spokesperson of God himself, who exhorts his 
people to a drastic change of attitude. 
 Judah and Israel have turned away from YHWH and the consequences are 
in front of anyone who is capable of seeing them: not only does impiety run rampant 
everywhere, but social injustice - its direct consequence - has been 
possessed of both Hebrew kingdoms in equal measure (ch. 1-2). Hence the 
prophet, imitating the style of his aforementioned contemporaries, did not 
hesitate to directly accuse those responsible, the leaders of the people, 
those who should have been paragons and examples of virtue; the nation 
It will never be better than those who direct it (chap. 3). This explains the hard tones 
with which the whole book is written, so much so that on occasions it has been 
compared to the most seasoned social revolutionaries of the different 
eras of history, more than one of which it will have served, let us not doubt it, 
of model. 
 But we would be wrong if we only focused on Micah's prophecy 
under this prism. Interwoven with its most incisive messages against 
corruption and evil of Judah and Israel and their leaders, hope appears. 
Micah is especially known for two key passages: 4:1-5, where he predicts 
the universal reign of God, manifestation of divine mercy for all 
the peoples, who will go to Mount Zion in search of the divine word; and 5:2, 
in which he anticipates the birth of the Messiah in Bethlehem Ephrathah. The first one 
also find, and with identical words, in the book of Isaiah 2:1-4, what has 
raised the question of priority between the two prophets or, perhaps better, whether 
both have not been nourished by a common source; the second, for its part, 
It will be consecrated forever in Mt. 2:6 as a messianic oracle. both 
texts proclaim that God's conflict with his people has a solution. God 
demands of the Israelites of the north and the south an attitude of total consecration that 
have its repercussions on daily life and on our relationships with each other (6:8). 

76

On the other hand, he issues a promise of unparalleled value: he will bury the sins of 
his people in the sea, so that he will remember them no more (7:18-19). 
 Hence, despite the time that has passed since its writing until today, the 
book of Micah is accessible to today's reader, since its message reaches the 
deepest concerns of man of all time.

Nahum of Elcos. A proper name and a toponym, undoubtedly its 
place of origin, although for us it is very difficult to locate 
(the mention of Judah in 1:15 would seem to place Nahum among the 
Jewish prophets, but not everyone understands it that way, 
especially in attention to 2:2, where it seems to speak of the 
northern kingdom of Israel). It is all we know of the prophet who since 
The first verse of this book declares that its oracles are directed against 
Nineveh, the great capital of the hitherto all-powerful Assyrian Empire and terror 
of the nations. The clear issuance of divine judgment on Assyrian power and its 
imminent destruction allows us to assume that Nahum exercises his ministry 
horse between the 8th and 7th centuries BC. C., which makes it possible 
contemporary of Isaiah and Micah, perhaps of Amos and Hosea.  
As Obadiah would later do, Nahum is called to prophesy 
against a foreign people, an enemy of Israel and, therefore, of God. Hence 
The images used by the prophet are of great stylistic value: they describe 
an unparalleled cataclysm as a result of a divine decree that puts an end to 
the tyranny of an essentially cruel nation, whose disappearance from the horizon 
history is a cause of joy among men (3:19). 
Nahum's prophecy has sometimes been accused of conveying a 
image of God that does not correspond to the revelation of the gospel of Christ. 
Say that YHWH is an avenging God, who holds a permanent grudge against 
with his adversaries (1:2) or that he will not take revenge twice on his enemies 
(1:9), is, in the opinion of some, to place it on the same level as the petty 
divinities of the pagan pantheons. It could even be understood as a 
justification of xenophobia or incitement to radical hatred against foreigners. 
But such statements only look at the superficial, without going too deep. 
in the core of the message or in its vital medium. Chapters 2 and 3 describe with 
without equal skill all the evil of Nineveh (and several capital cities of 
other empires of the past) and their cruelty against the weakest, so that 
The whole book of Nahum becomes a withering plea against the 
oppression and destructive imperialisms. It is not that YHWH hates the Assyrians, 
nor to the towns mentioned in chapter. 3, if not he hates 
injustice and oppressive abuse of certain political states. Nahum's prophecy 
is not a manual of dogmatic theology about the essence of God, but a 
punctual and very specific proclamation of a devastating divine judgment against a 

78

military and political power that has gone beyond the way it has treated 
to the surrounding towns.  
Hence the perennial relevance of the message of this unknown prophet in 
so much so that vindication of the elementary rights of the weak before the 
powerful, because God does not tolerate the suffering of the little ones nor will he endure it 
indefinitely. Nahum is a book whose reading, except for those figures 
typical of its cultural environment and its historical moment, continues to remind us 
that God is the only Sovereign, and that no human power has the right to 
oppress his fellow men.

Habakkuk's prophecy is presented to modern Bible readers 
like a little jewel. Small for its size, only three 
chapters of short length, but enormous for their magnificent and 
careful composition (evidence of priestly circles 
linked to the temple of Jerusalem and to which the 
prophet?) and, in a very special way, for its unparalleled content. The force 
declarative nature of its message is such that it completely eclipses its author. In fact, 
We really know nothing about the person of the prophet except his 
name. The text does not offer any information about his family or his place of origin. 
It is only possible for us to deduce the period in which he exercises his ministry: the 
mention of the Chaldeans (1:6ff.) as enemies and destroyers of Judah tells us 
allows us to place Habakkuk among those who lived through the end of the Jewish state and the 
taking and destruction of Jerusalem and the temple by the hands of the Babylonians the year 
586 BC C. Habakkuk was, therefore, a contemporary of Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the 
young prince Daniel, Zephaniah and Obadiah. 
 Habakkuk's prophecy is presented as a statement of fact, the 
threatening invasion c village; a clear complaint to God for such a situation, 
understood by the prophet as totally unjust; the surprising answer 
divine, and to conclude, a beautiful psalm of praise, which occupies the third 
chapter of the book, and in which a horizon of hope is drawn for the 
people of the Lord. Habakkuk must have been part of the Jews who lived 
confident in the security of the divine promises to the dynasty of David and in the 
presence of the temple in the city of Jerusalem as a guarantee of preservation 
of the Jewish state, without discerning that God is not tied to political institutions 
of this world and that its promises may very well be fulfilled beyond the 
narrow limits of the immediate human horizon. Hence the immense value of 
the divine response to the prophet when he tells him that he whose soul is not upright 
proud, but the righteous will live by his faithfulness (2:4), words that, cited by 
Saint Paul in Rio. 1:17, would become many centuries later the inspiration of 
one of the largest religious movements in Christian history. God 
confronts the complaining prophet Habakkuk with a new situation, with a change 
total paradigm; what seemed immovable is not in reality, and there is 
new fields to explore, new realities that point to the integrity of the 
believer for himself, regardless of the decisions or actions of 
who lead the people. In this sense, the prophecy of Habakkuk, the same 
than that of his contemporaries Jeremiah or Ezekiel, emphasizes the 
responsibility of the individual before God and before others. 

80

There is nothing strange, then, that the book of Habakkuk is for the 
current reader of the Holy Scriptures of a singular modernity, and that his 
content is so close to the gospel. Habakkuk offers hope when 
there is none and it sketches a picture of blessedness only possible for those who, 
As God tells them, they live a life of fidelity, that is, of faith.

Although it cannot be said that the short book of Zephaniah is one of 
the most cited or best known by the current reader of the Bible, 
It must be admitted that its message, both in terms of its form 
as well as its content, is of singular beauty, and enjoyed in 
other times of great preaching, as evidenced by the fact that 
inspired the medieval author of the Latin song Dies irae, referring to the final judgment.  
 The prophet Zephaniah exercises his ministry during the reign of Josiah in 
Judah (1:1), which makes him a contemporary of Jeremiah and other great figures 
religious of the moment. He must have, without a doubt, witnessed the destruction of 
Jerusalem, which, according to some, must have caused him greater pain than 
other servants of God for the fact - it would seem to be assumed - of being a prophet 
courtier of very high birth, perhaps of royal lineage, as the 
first verse of the book (direct descendant of King Hezekiah?). Whether or not 
Thus, the truth is that Zephaniah has the greatest genealogy of all the prophets -
authors of the Bible, something that is not common and that could very well indicate a 
privileged position of his family in the midst of the Jewish society of the time. 
 His message is as clear as it is brief and concise: God has established a day 
in which he will judge the injustices and impiety of the nations, beginning with 
Judah herself. But all this pre-apocalyptic language of judgment and destruction 
(1:14-16) must be understood in its vital environment not so much as an anticipation of the 
end of the world (Christian doctrine of the final judgment), how much rather the end of the 
autonomy of the peoples around Israel, delivered by a special 
divine disposition in the hands of the new emerging power that is Babylon. So 
Therefore, the day of wrath anticipated by Zephaniah will be the conquest of Jerusalem and the 
end of the kingdom of Judah, events that for the people of God imply the conclusion 
of an entire world, the end of an era that will never return. Said with others 
In other words, the God of Zephaniah is a God who neither tolerates impiety nor endures 
human evil, which he puts an end to in a fulminant way, dragging 
his own people into captivity. 
  However, and following the same line as the rest of the 
ancient prophets, Zephaniah also proclaims redemption and 
hope. The third chapter of his book presents, all wrapped in the garb 
characteristic of the whole work, a proclamation of redemption: the people of God, 
although severely punished by the Lord because of his infidelity, he will return 
from captivity to enter an era of peace and blessing. In the same way that 
Divine judgment is a reality from which no nation can escape, 

82

God's mercy is always present. God sends the prophet to 
admonish and exhort a human group that has departed from it, not with the 
purpose of destroying it, but of restoring it. 
 Zephaniah, in this way, does not depart from the general line marked by 
the prophets who live before the restoration. Hence his message continues 
being encouraging for believers of our days.

With the short book of the prophet Haggai (or Haggai, as transcribed 
some editions of the Bible) we fully breathe the atmosphere of 
the restoration of the Jewish people immediately after the 
Babylonian captivity. The first verse of the writing tells us 
clearly that Judea is subject to Persian power, at the same time 
time that marks the two recipients of the prophecy: Zerubbabel, the governor 
Jewish, and his direct collaborator, the high priest Joshua;  that is, the 
civil authorities (by Persian delegation) and religious authorities.  
 Haggai, like his friend Zechariah, seeks above all that 
the Jewish people recover their identity as beneficiaries of the ancient 
divine promises to Israel, for which it is imperative that the 
Temple of Jerusalem, dwelling place of God among men. but the reality 
presented in chap. 1 is disheartening: the inhabitants of the newly 
repopulated Jerusalem are concerned exclusively with their own well-being, for their 
houses, and ignore the temple, whose reconstruction, according to the 
first chapters of the book of Ezra, would have been hindered by the 
enemies of the Jews. Haggai's call will, therefore, have as its purpose 
convince an apathetic and selfish nation of the need to address 
primarily of the things of God. The reason is twofold: on the one hand, the people 
Jew can incur divine displeasure (and he knows well from his recent history 
what this can entail!), but on the other hand the design of God's will 
is that the new temple that is to be rebuilt has a destiny assigned 
glorious, much larger than the one the temple of 
Solomon. The words of the prophet regarding this matter, beautiful as 
few, are transformed in this way, especially in the Christian tradition 
from the Vulgate, in a messianic oracle of profound scope (2:6-7). 
 It is, therefore, the permanent tension between the restorative ideal and the 
reality of a people that does not seem interested in responding to expectations 
marked, which allows us to understand the whole book of Haggai. Esd. 5:1 
mentions Haggai and Zechariah by name, and the rest of the chapter allows 
understand that his prophetic proclamations were successful, but this does not obviate the 
condition of the Hierosolimitan Jews that Haggai describes.  
  The book of Haggai concludes with a very direct oracle to Zerubbabel 
(2:20-23), whom God himself declares to have chosen. Prince of the house of 
David, Zerubbabel represents the hopes of the Jewish people in a return of the 
historical monarchy. Haggai's text, however, does not seem to point to a 

84

independent political solution of the Persian Empire, but to a purely 
rebuilding the house of God.  
 Written simply, without the apocalyptic overtones of other prophetic works, 
The book of Haggai becomes accessible to the modern reader and can captivate him, 
since the situation he poses, mutatis mutandis, is very similar to that of 
our hedonistic and selfish societies, for which God and his will 
They always turn out to be something very secondary and totally dispensable.

For the modern scholar and reader of the Holy Scriptures, the book of 
Zechariah is presented as a compilation of unknowns of no 
Too easy solution. In relation to the distribution of its texts, the 
Current criticism distinguishes three well-differentiated parts, attributable to, 
least, three different hands: Proto-Zechariah (ch. 1-8), Deutero-Zechariah (ch. 9-
11) and Trito-Zechariah (ch. 12-14), of which only the first would be the work of the 
prophet of this name, perhaps a Levite or a priest, contemporary of 
Haggai and champion of the Jewish restoration in Jerusalem (1:1). The other two, 
think, they would be the work of disciples of Zechariah, although perhaps they collected oracles 
of other prophets, even earlier (Mt. 27:9 -10 quotes Zech. 11:12 -13 attributing 
these words to Jeremiah). As far as his style is concerned, clearly 
apocalyptic (especially in the visions of the first six chapters and in the 
Trito-Zechariah), and what concerns its content, let the words of Saint 
Jerome when he states that Zechariah is the most difficult book of all to understand. 
the whole Bible. 
 But none of these obstacles prevent us from understanding that, as a whole, 
Zechariah is a proclamation of hope in the midst of moments and situations  
difficult times, when Jews returning to their homeland face a great 
hostility. Both the eight visions of the first six chapters and the 
Later oracles refer to God's exquisite care for his 
people and their city of Jerusalem. At no time is the reality of 
some conditions are adverse, but all of Heaven is committed to the 
rehabilitation of the remnant of Judah. Zechariah, like the book of Daniel, 
shows the reality of a world parallel to the terrestrial one, the celestial world where 
angels execute the designs of God, a sphere in which the 
Human events are already predetermined forever, since the decrees  
of the Most High are unappealable. Not even Satan's hostility against 
priesthood of Israel (ch. 3) will have no negative effect: that which God has 
decreed and established concerning his people will be fulfilled without fail.  
Even the oracles of the last chapters, especially those of the Tritus -
Zechariah (who has lent himself so much to the overflowing fantasy of some 
interpreters of all times), despite its shocking images of trial and 
mass destruction, constitute in themselves a vindication of the people of God 
before the hostile nations of this world, as well as a patent reaffirmation of the 
power of YHWH. 

86

Furthermore, and in a very special way in the book of Zechariah, the 
messianic oracles that New Testament evangelists will quote 
literally applying them to the Lord Jesus: images such as the triumphant king who 
enters the city humbly riding a donkey (9:9) or the wounded shepherd and 
The scattered sheep (13:7) are now part of universal Christian culture. 
 Enigmatic book if there is one, Zechariah is a universal reference 
obligatory part of Old Testament prophecy, not always easy to read, but 
captivating and challenging, since the Word of God captivates and continually challenges the 
hearts of men with his message of salvation and restoration.

With the book of Malachi not only does the so-called Books come to an end. 
Prophetic, but the Christian Old Testament canon is closed, 
so that it gives way to the New Testament. This makes Malachi a 
very special writing that also raises other problems. The first, the 
distribution of your text; Some Bible versions, such as RVR60, separate the 
last six verses of chap. 3 and make them a chap. 4, while others 
They present the book with only three chapters. The second, the personality of your 
author; 1:1 does not offer any information that allows us to know who it is: neither 
affiliation nor place of origin, nor time in which he exercises the prophetic ministry, we 
They are known. The problem is that the only name he offers, Malachi, does not 
It appears to be a proper name, but rather a title: “messenger of YHWH.” 
Although several possible names have been considered for identification, the 
balance seems to lean in favor of the scribe and priest Ezra, one of the 
great protagonists of the restoration, although it is not a proposal that 
please all specialists. 
 Be that as it may, the author of this unique writing is someone who lives 
concerned about the conditions of the priesthood of the newly restored temple of 
Jerusalem, among whose components he detects an offensive neglect towards the 
Lord, especially when the name of the God of Israel is already something known and 
appreciated among the nations (1:11). Hence Malachi's message has 
its main purpose is to exhort the sacred hierarchies of the sanctuary 
hierosolimitano, and the people as a whole, to a life of fidelity and obedience 
to the ritual and ceremonial prescriptions of the Law, return of tithes 
included (3:6-12), which places us perfectly well in the time of the 
Restoration. 
 The finishing touch to Malachi's prophecy, however, is provided by his 
messianic aspect. Like Haggai and other prophets, he speaks of a coming of the 
Lord to his temple, but with the addition that a messenger will precede him (3:1), 
all of this framed in a background of judgment, the Day of the Lord or Yom Adonay, 
in the style of the most classic prophets from before the deportation to Babylon. but 
the emphasis on the figure of the herald of God, identified as the prophet 
Elijah (4:5 -6 or 3:23 -24, depending on the editions), would be understood by Jesus and the 
evangelists as a prediction of the ministry of John the Baptist (Mk. 9:11 -
13; Lc. 1:17). Thus, in the current arrangement of our Bibles 
Christians, the Old Covenant would conclude by predicting the coming of the Forerunner before 
of that of the Lord himself, thus linking with the evangelical stories narrated by the

It is usually designated in the Protestant and evangelical world with the 
qualifier of “apocrypha”—Greek term that means 
“hidden”, “occult” — a series of books never accepted as 
Sacred Scripture for Palestinian Judaism, but closely linked to 
the Old Testament, and which are present for the first time in the 
Greek version of the LXX or Septuagint, and later in the Latin Vulgate, as well 
as in the Coptic and Syriac versions. They are also found in the versions  
current versions of the Bible published under the auspices of the Roman Catholic Church, 
the Orthodox and Eastern Churches, or the so-called interdenominational bibles. In 
All these editions preferably receive the designation of “books.” 
deuterocanonical”—also a Hellenic word whose meaning is “of a 
second canon”—which is much more adjusted to its intrinsic reality than the 
first designation. If in the Catholic, Orthodox or Eastern versions of the 
Bible appear within the Old Testament occupying different places 
according to the edition, in the interdenominational ones they are presented rather as a 
independent section between the Old and New Testaments. 
 Protestant editions of the Bible do not generally publish them 
since the beginning of the 19th century due to an orchestrated campaign against them 
by certain Calvinist or Reformed churches, although the reality is that 
the biblical editions that saw the light of day in the Reformation (the German Bible of 
Luther, the Spanish ones of Casiodoro de Reyna and Cipriano de Valera, or the first  
edition of the English King James Version, to mention only the best known) the 
they contained. In fact, the reformer Martin Luther considered them a type of 
pious literature and good to read, although not totally comparable to 
Old Testament canonical; and the thirty-nine articles of Communion 
Anglican, although they do not consider them inspired like the writings 
(proto)canonical Old Testament, see in them a type of literature 
edifying and good for believers. 
 The different apologetic reasons why the world 
Protestant and evangelical do not accept them as full-fledged biblical books, as 
as is usually alleged in works published for the use of seminarians or believers 
In general, today they are not sustained as easily as in other times of 
greater ignorance of biblical sciences. In fact, much of what 
was stated about them actually applies to many canonical writings of the 

90

Old and New Testament. For this reason, it is increasingly spreading among the s 
Protestant and evangelical scholars the idea that biblical editions 
current ones should imitate those of the Reformation, in which they were included. 
 Without entering into this type of disquisitions, which go beyond our study, 
we recognize in them a natural continuation of the Old Testament  
composed of works of historical, narrative, prophetic and wisdom nature, 
written mostly in Greek and outside Palestine (fundamental reason for the 
Jewish rejection), which exude a spirituality very close to Christianity and 
impregnated with Hellenistic philosophy, in addition to occasionally offering data 
historical records of great value.  The fact that its authors are for the most part 
unknown to us (they must have been in ancient times) in no way 
diminishes its great testimonial, stylistic and even theological value, so 
have well earned their place within the set of biblical literature, they 
whether or not it recognizes its canonical authority. 
 We present them in the following order: Tobias (Tob.), Judith (Jdt.), Esther 
Greek (Est. Gr.), Wisdom (Sab.), Ecclesiasticus (Eclos.), Baruch (Bar.), Daniel 
Greek (Dn. Gr.), 1 Maccabees (1 Maccabees) and 2 Maccabees (2 Maccabees).  the bibles 
Classical Spanish Protestants designate them as “deuterocanonical” and, either 
include them in the Old Testament (Bear Bible) or place them in a 
intermediate section between the Old and New Testaments (Cántaro Bible). 
We also add three very old works that were present in the 
editions of the Vulgate and in the first Protestant versions of the Reformation: 
Prayer of Manasseh (Or. Man.), 3 Esdras (3 Esd.) and 4 Esdras (4 Esd. or Ap. Esd.), 
which the Bear and Pitcher Bibles indicate as “apocrypha.”

Also called the Book of Tobit in some modern editions of the 
Bible, presents all the characteristics of a Jewish folk tale of the 
time of the Maccabean revolt (2nd century BC) or perhaps a little before, and 
whose purpose is essentially didactic: to promote piety, especially 
prayer and works of charity (burying the dead and, above all, almsgiving to 
the needy and destitute).  Written in all probability in Palestine and in 
Aramaic language by an author unknown to us, it is only 
accessible by Greek translation in two versions, one short and one long, with 
more details. The latter, translated into Latin in the Vulgate and then into the languages 
moderns, it is the one that is mostly published today in current Bibles. 
 Supposedly set at the time of the deportation of Israel 
northern Assyria (8th-7th centuries BC), presents two scenarios: on the one 
side, the city of Nineveh, capital of the Assyrians, where Tobias (or Tobit) resides, 
its protagonist, with his wife and son Tobias in the middle of a community of 
captive compatriots in which he exercises the virtues of an Israelite faithful to 
God even at the risk of his own life, and where as a result of an ill-fated 
accident loses sight; on the other, Ecbatana, a city of Media, where they reside 
some relatives of Tobias with Sara, his daughter, who lives tormented by the 
demon Asmodeus, enemy of marriage and murderer of all her husbands 
when they enter the bridal chamber with her on their wedding day. After a 
captivating story in which different adventures, travels, business, 
spells and love, Sara marries the young Tobias in Ecbatana, who 
He returns safely to Nineveh and cures his father of his blindness by applying a 
remedy obtained on the trip.  The end of the play introduces us to the once young 
Tobias, now old, with Sara his wife and numerous offspring, who after having  
buried his parents and his in-laws who died in good old age, he abandons 
Nineveh, of whose fall and destruction he is a happy witness, thus seeing the fulfillment of the 
oracles of the prophets of Israel. 
 The book of Tobias introduces on the scene, in the form of a young Israelite 
called Azariah, to the (arc)angel Raphael, one of the seven holy celestial beings

For more than a millennium and a half, Christians have given the name 
New Testament to the set of twenty-seven canonical sacred writings 
that make up the second part of the Holy Bible. They saw the light in a 
relatively short period of time, between the middle of the 1st century AD. C. and the 
first decades of the II, approximately, in accordance with the most

In these books we find, basically, the testimony of faith of the first

 Indeed, it is the historical reality of the man Jesus of Nazareth —

conception of God, the world and human reality itself. In Jesus

merciful Lord capable of delivering his own Son to death for the 
redemption of the human race. Nothing can be the same as before, because the Kingdom of

with that same Jesus who will return at the end of time in the clouds of the 
heavens in order to collect his people.
