own Christian communities, it is said, from the final decades of the first century, 
when the apostle Saint Paul had already died. It actually appears in 1 
Timothy a certain clerical structure (3:1-13) different from what is found 
in the oldest Pauline epistles, and there is no lack of allusion to heretical doctrines 
adverse to the gospel that are already emerging, one would say, within the 
communities, endangering the integrity of the gospel (1:3-11; 4:1-5).  
 Hence the message of this epistle is a constant call to the 
presbyter Timothy so that he is not only able to confront those false 
teachings and bring to good fruition the congregation over which he exercises his 
care, but also so that it can organize the life of the Church according to 
to a pattern of order desired by God. This epistle exudes exhortations to 
a practical piety embodied in the lives of believers, regardless 
of what their responsibilities, ages or private circumstances are.  The 
Christian existence is conceived as a battle (6:12) in which all the faithful 
They participate inspired by the most sublime. Just as in 2 Thes. 2:7 alluded to 
to the mystery of iniquity, here the apostolic instruction speaks of the mystery of 
piety, which is the proper work of Christ in his incarnation, death, resurrection and 
ascension, quoting for this what must undoubtedly have been a song of the 
primitive communities (3:16). 
 The chaps. 5 and 6 contain very direct advice and commands for Timothy 
as a pastor of the community, and in them we find basic principles 
which the Christian clergy of all centuries has considered as the foundation 
unavoidable part of ministerial praxis. We should not have the slightest doubt 
that, from the direct hand of Saint Paul or his later disciples, in them 

150

we find the authoritative voice of the Apostle of the Gentiles instructing those who 
He had been one of his most direct collaborators in evangelization. 
 The style in which the Epistle 1 Timothy is written is what 
clear enough to be read and understood easily even 
in our days, at the same time deep enough to 
continue to constitute a fundamental element in the inspiration of life 
pious, both for clerics and laymen.

A very ancient Christian tradition has seen in this Epistle 2 Timothy 
something like the spiritual testament of the apostle Saint Paul. Written, 
it is said, from the last prison in which the faithful Apostle of the 
Gentiles lived his final days in Rome before his execution by order of l 
reigning emperor Nero Caesar (4:6-8), comes to show, in addition to the 
affection of Saint Paul for his disciple and friend Timothy, a whole series of 
exhortations to Christian life and ministerial service, understood as a 
authentic militia Christi (chap. 2). 
 Current exegesis, however, while recognizing the Apostle's hand in 
the basic materials of the writing and in the final greetings to very people 
specifics of his circle, he clearly opts for late writing, 
after the death of Saint Paul. Thus, the letter would have been written by 
one of his disciples, for his school, of which the text itself would present 
certain irrefutable evidence. 
 Like 1 Timothy, this epistle appears written in a style 
very loose, easy to read and understand even for believers in our 
days. The themes it addresses are, on the other hand, universal.  The situation 
ecclesiasticism that appears between the lines is that of well-known communities. 
established in which there are, however, groups that are lost in 
absurd discussions about inconsequential topics (2:10,23) or also 
individuals who have fallen completely into heresy and have dragged others into the 
perdition (2:17-18), without being able to specify exactly what kind of 
heretical movement is about. The situation of the Apostle, who awaits his 
last sentence, on the other hand, colors the entire epistle with a climate of certain 
tension: the persecution of believers is at the doors (3:12-13), as 
consequence of the current times. The chap. 3 makes it clear 
that there exists among Christians of the moment the full awareness of living in the s 
end times, in which the increase of evil and perversion will be more 
evident than ever (Domitian's persecution, especially highlighted in 
Asia Minor?) All of this affects the fact that Timothy, as pastor of the 
Church, must remain firm and be an encouragement and an example to others, 
for God calls his workers to be brave (1:7). 
In the midst of all these exhortations and advice sprinkled with 
doctrinal statements of the Pauline school, data also appear 
personal details of Timothy that are not found anywhere else in the New 
Testament: the name of his mother and grandmother, both believers (1:5), and his 

152

appear to have good knowledge of the Holy Scriptures (the Old Testament), 
which he had received from childhood (3:15), all of which constitutes useful baggage 
for an arduous ministry. The Apostle clearly declares that he desires his 
presence (4:9,13,21), thus showing the great friendship that unites them. 
All of these features contribute to making the Epistle 2 Timothy one of 
perhaps the most endearing writings of the Corpus Paulinum and perhaps the one in which 
the Apostle of the Gentiles appears with his kindest, most human face. The 
man overcomes the theologian to show, in addition to his most 
intimate, kinder, a deep faith that does not abandon him even in the last 
moments of his earthly existence.

Last and shortest of the pastoral letters, the Epistle to Titus appears 
addressed to a collaborator of the apostle Saint Paul who exercises the sacred 
ministry on the island of Crete and who, it seems, would be in charge 
several congregations, a diocese (1:5) in which he was to establish elders  
(presbyters) and put things in order, given the idiosyncrasies of the inhabitants 
from that place, believers included (1:12-13). Just like what happened with the 
two epistles to Timothy, although Christian Antiquity had no qualms 
In considering the Epistle to Titus as a Pauline letter, current exegesis 
rather classified as “deuteropauline” for the reasons already expressed 
previously. In the same way as in the rest of the Pastoral Epistles, the 
letter to Titus contains (who could doubt it today?) literary materials 
authentic from the pen of the Apostle of the Gentiles, with information about his 
person and the places where he is located of which there is no trace in 
Acts of the Apostles or in any other writing of the New Testament.  Your 
definitive writing, however, comes from the hand of a for us  
anonymous disciple of the Pauline school who would have lived at the end of the first 
century of our Era, when the Church appears already institutionalized and its 
concerns are different from the early Christian movement led by the 
apostles. 
 The background of the epistle is a Church in which there are problems 
generated by those who deviate from the truth following very 
particular and apparently rigorous of the Scriptures (1:14 -15; 3:9), before which the 
apostolic advice is firm: admonishment and expulsion from the community if necessary 
necessary (3:10 -11). Since these are not questions of mere ritualism 
Jewish, as was the case of the believers to whom the Epistle to the 
Galatians, but moral and political issues appear intermingled. 
speculative, perhaps the Epistle to Titus (along with Colossians and 1 Timothy 
within the Corpus Paulinum) gives us one of the first testimonies of the 
presence of the Gnostic ferment in the Christian communities of the late l 
1st century. 
 Be that as it may, the keynote of this writing is the insistence on order  
internal to the Church, the sound doctrine centered on Christ Jesus and his salvation by 
pure grace with universal tones unusual in the set of 
New Testament writings (2:11), and the exhortation to a life of service to 
others within the Christian community, things of which no one can be 

154

exempt, neither by position or responsibility, nor by age or any other 
circumstance (chap. 2). 
 Written in a clean, clear and concise style at the same time, it is 
of a letter that is very easy and comfortable to read for the man of our days. 
The concepts that it conveys, despite the space-time distance, seem to us 
accessible to those of us who live in the 21st century, and even use the questions raised 
and the problems raised are, mutatis mutandis, identical to those that today 
we can live. 
 Thus it is understood that it is a particularly apostolic writing. 
useful for devotional and informative commentary on Christian life, as 
evidenced by the abundant literature of our days in which it occupies a place 
very prominent.

Without a doubt the shortest writing of those that make up the Corpus Paulinum, this 
epistle, which some commentators once classified within the 
Pastorals, is considered by current exegesis as a direct work of 
Saint Paul and written from prison (v. 1), although without being able to specify well 
which one. Addressed to a believing friend, Philemon, perhaps a priest in the city of 
Colossae (v. 2), constitutes a milestone in the Christian perception of the problem 
of slavery, although there have been some who point it out as a great 
disappointment, undoubtedly due to not having properly understood the real content of this 
written. 
 The basic theme is different from everything we find in the whole of the 
Corpus Paulinum: we do not read in it anything about internal problems of any 
community, nor do we come across doctrinal expositions, 
general exhortations to the Christian life or refutations of heresies. Saint Paul 
intercedes with his friend and companion Philemon for Onesimus, a Christian believer 
converted by the Apostle's ministry, but at the same time a fugitive slave 
of the house of Philemon, with all that this entailed in society and 
Roman legislation of the time. The Apostle begs forgiveness for Onesimus and 
his reception in the house of his former master, but now as a brother in faith. 
 The fact that Saint Paul does not demand the freedom of Onesimus and his 
emancipation before the Roman laws by Philemon has constituted for 
some a terrible impact: Saint Paul, they say, should have taken advantage of this 
unique situation to proclaim liberation in the name of the gospel of Christ 
of the slaves. But it is difficult to suppose that a man of the first century, as was the 
Apostle, such concepts would be raised. Slavery had cemented the 
human societies, eastern and western, since time immemorial, of 
so that none of the great thinkers had questioned it. In the 
Jewish sphere, the Mosaic legislation was not opposed to it as a system. And not even 
Not even Jesus himself had suggested the slightest alteration in this 
sense. Saint Paul, logically, was not going to break that line of thought. but 
does something much more effective than a general manumission petition, whose 
The result would not have been the one desired: he demands Philemon, the aggrieved master, the 
recognition of Onesimus as his brother in faith (vv. 15-16), his equal before 
God, occupy the position you occupy in society and before human laws. 
With his words Saint Paul deals a greater blow to slavery as a system 
social than the revolt of Spartacus, undoubtedly still very present in that 
moment, and thus lays the foundations for what will one day allow many Christians 

156

openly confront the scourge of slavery to abolish it 
definitely. 
 This is why the Epistle to Philemon, properly understood, contains a proclamation 
revolutionary whose scope goes beyond the first century, even our century 
XXI, and not only against classical slavery, but against all its forms and 
manifestations, ancient and modern. Hence it is an easy writing to 
read, always respecting its vital environment, and even particularly endearing 
for believers today.

We can say without fear of being wrong that the so-called Epistle to the 
Hebrews constitutes one of the greatest enigmas of the New Testament. 
Although it has traditionally been considered the last of the 
writings that make up the Corpus Paulinum, their real authorship is unknown, and already 
It was so in the first centuries of the Christian Era. Even though the editions 
ancient versions of the Bible designate it as “Epistle of Saint Paul [Apostle] to the 
Hebrews”, no one knows who actually wrote it. A multitude of 
names, from Saint Paul himself (thus John Calvin) to Priscilla, wife of 
Aquila, passing, among others, through Saint Luke the Evangelist, Barnabas or the learned 
Apollos, the latter being a very expensive proposal to Martin Luther and several specialists 
of our days. The only thing we know for sure is that it is a written 
very elaborate, much more than the other Pauline epistles, and in a Greek 
excellent, comparable to that of San Lucas. 
 A similar problem arises in relation to its recipients, who 
They appear to be Jews and even priests, according to some commentators. 
noted, of those who from the first days of the Church obeyed the 
faith (Acts 6:7), without lacking those who think of adherents to the sect of Qumram 
converted to Christianity. The only certain thing, according to the last verses of the 
chap. 13, would be the starting point of the writing, Italy, and possibly within the 
circle of disciples of Saint Paul (allusion to Timothy). So much lack of certainty 
caused the Epistle to the Hebrews to have problems entering the 
biblical canon, and that it did not fully do so until the end of Antiquity. 
 Despite all this, its message is extraordinary: it is presented more as a 
sermon that, like a letter itself, a reasoning 
masterfully developed to exalt Christ, as the Son of God 
declared superior to Moses and the angels themselves (ch. 1 and 3), and enthroned 
as perpetual high priest in heaven before God the Father (ch. 7-10). The 
The author demonstrates that he knows very well, very closely even, everything related to the 
cult in the Jewish sanctuary, still active at the time he composed this 
written, which indicates a writing prior to the year 70 AD. C. Your arguments to 
favor of a change of priesthood and law allow us to assume that it is directed 
especially to Jews converted to the gospel, but, for reasons of 
us unknown, tending to take a step back and return to their old 
cultic system. 
 The author's superior knowledge of the Holy Scriptures 
It is also evident in chap. 11, traditionally known as “the 

158

chapter of the heroes of the faith”, where this virtue that has colored the 
History of Salvation from the first moment, from the patriarchs 
antediluvians to the persecutions suffered by the Jews in the period 
intertestamental (the author seems to allude to the deuterocanonical 2 Maccabees and the 
apocryphal or pseudoepigraphic Assumption of Isaiah). Jesus is the fulfillment 
full of everything that the Old Testament presented, and he who gives it his 
true sense. Hence the final chapters (12 -13) contain valuable 
exhortations to the Christian life, a life of faith and service and obedience to 
God and men. 
 It is not very easy for today's reader to delve into the 
motley world of the Epistle to the Hebrews. You can lose the thread 
reasoning without great complications, which requires very careful reading 
and a high level of concentration. Yet the greatness of Christ remains 
very evident with a simple superficial reading.  
 Regardless of who were its real author, its recipients, the 
date or place of composition, the Epistle to the Hebrews is one of the writings 
most commented and explained in the entire New Testament, and rightly so. Despite 
doubts of the ancient Church, its place in the biblical canon is more than 
guaranteed.

content:
The remaining books that make up our canonical New Testament are mostly of the epistolary genre, the so-called Catholic or Universal Epistles, a set of seven letters that, unlike the 
Corpus Paulinum, do not have a specific recipient, but are addressed in 
principle to all the Christian faithful: Epistle of James (James), 1 Saint 
Peter (1 P.), 2 Saint Peter (2 P.), 1 Saint John (1 Jn.), 2 Saint John (2 Jn.), 3 Saint John 
(3 Jn.) and Saint Jude (Jud.) ; only 2 and 3 Jn. could be the exception to this 
characteristic, but they have not been separated from the group of the Epistles 
Universal. To this collection of seven letters is added the Apocalypse (Rev.), 
very special book with which the New Testament canon closes. 
 From the first moment, these writings posed problems for the 
Church, since they were not recognized by everyone as canonical works. Only 1 
Saint Peter and 1 Saint John were received without discussion and considered 
apostolic epistles from the first moment. The others and the Apocalypse 
It took centuries to be fully accepted within the general canon by 
very different reasons. Hence they have been considered in certain circles 
exegetical and theological books such as “deuterocanonical books”, “antilegomena” or 
a second canon, without the same authority as the New Testament writings 
not discussed by the first Christian communities (“protocanonical books” 
or “homologous”). 
 In our days, both the Universal Epistles and the book of the 
Apocalypse are the subject of important studies, given that their contents 
respective reflect the feeling and understanding of the gospel of certain sectors 
not inconsiderable aspects of early Christianity. Finally, his presence in the 
New Testament canon also implies a fact that has not always been 
calibrated in the best way: the diversity of opinions or points of view 
existing in the ancient Church and that, in a certain way, anticipate the later 
divisions of historical Christianity. Just as, it is said, the epistolary 
Pauline, together with the Lucan work, would present the basic guidelines of 
what centuries later would be Protestant theology, the Fourth Gospel, the 
Johannine epistles and the Apocalypse would echo a very 
close to the Eastern Orthodox spirituality of our days; the gospel 
according to Saint Mark and Epistles 1 and 2 Peter (some include here also the 
Lucan work), would show the beginnings of Roman Catholic theology, and the Gospel 
according to Saint Matthew and the epistles of James and Saint Jude would offer us 
touches of the now disappeared primitive Orthodox Judeo-Christianity, which 

160

had such importance in the beginnings of the Church and that lasted during 
the first century and part of the second, to die after having led to Ebionism, 
declaredly heretical. In this sense, this important final part of the New 
Testament would come to influence the ecumenical aspect of the twenty-seven writings 
sacred parts of apostolic Christianity. 
 Be that as it may, the Universal Epistles and the Apocalypse, even 
recognizing its undeniable direct dependence on Evangelical History and the 
Apostle Saint Paul, constitute a section worthy of being taken into account in their own right. 
same when reading and studying the New Testament.

Called a “straw epistle” by the Reformer Martin Luther, who did not 
valued as a truly canonical letter, it is a writing that has always been 
lent to controversy. The fact that its author is James (1:1), 
traditionally identified as James the Just, brother of Jesus and 
first bishop of Jerusalem, who died a martyr shortly before the destruction of the 
city by Roman troops, far from giving it authority in Christendom 
primitive, relegated it to oblivion in a good part of the communities, given that 
represented a thought directly opposite to that of the apostle Saint Paul 
(2:14-26), despite the subsequent efforts of the concordists who have 
intended—without much success, to be honest—to alleviate or explain the 
differences convincingly. 
 If we add to this the curious feature that, except for the explicit mention of the 
first verse, the name of Jesus is conspicuous by its absence throughout the writing, 
in addition to the sententious style that permeates it, so close to that of the book of the 
Proverbs, it is perfectly understandable that more than one scholar has 
considered this epistle in itself a sermon composed in principle to be 
delivered in a Jewish synagogue, perhaps later adapted for the 
Judeo-Christian communities, in which it would be preferable not to mention Christ for 
his name and call him simply the Lord (5:16), but not a written 
genuinely Christian.  
 We would, however, make a serious mistake if, despite the evidence 
reviewed, we would pretend to ignore the value of a letter focused on 
concern for a life truly in accordance with God's will for us 
the believers. The faithful must be wise according to the meaning that this term has in the 
Bible (1:5 -6; 3:13 -18), so its existence must be marked by the 
submission to divine will (4:15), which will be reflected in total self-control 
(ch. 3). 
 An important feature of the Epistle of James is his judgment 
excessively negative about the rich and powerful, even reaching the 
prophetic tones of certain books of the Old Testament (2:1-13; 5:1-6). Without 
doubt, this shows communities composed of people rather 
simple and with few resources, in need of help (cf. the mentions of Saint 
Paul the Apostle to the poor of Jerusalem in the final chapters of 1 and 2 
Corinthians) and not very well treated by the upper classes of the society of the 
moment. James never declares that the possession of wealth is in itself something 
sinful, but he makes clear his abhorrence towards those who make them 

162

an end in themselves, neglecting the duty of charity towards others. 
disinherited, widows and orphans. 
 In short, the Epistle of James is a writing that is easy to 
reading and not complicated conceptual understanding. It never ceases to amaze, 
even not too pleasantly, many believers today 
affected by the Theology of Grace, given that its wording opposes 
openly to the Pauline postulates of justification by faith. But not for 
his exhortations to a practical pious life and to a 
real action in favor of the weakest, in which it stands as an authority 
coming from God and a call to a non-theoretical religiosity.

In the so-called Epistle 1 Saint Peter the oldest Christian traditions 
have recognized without any problem the authoritative voice of the Prince of 
the Apostles (1:1), writing from Rome—symbolically designated 
like Babylon—and most likely through his amanuensis Saint 
Mark (5:13).  This explains why it entered the New Testament canon from the 
first moment without problems and that enjoyed a good reputation as 
genuinely apostolic writing. 
 The epistle appears written in a particularly warm, affable, 
easy to read even for our contemporaries, so it has all the 
traces of an exhortation addressed by a loving father to his children. In no 
moment the apostle Saint Peter displays pretensions of authoritarianism throughout 
this writing, but rather he shows himself as someone especially humble 
and who lives at the service of others (5:1ff.), because the center of his life and his 
proclaims is the Lord Jesus Christ. Although the best known passage in this sense 
is, without a doubt, 2:4-8, in which Christ is presented before the listener-readers as 
the living stone that the builders rejected, the whole of the letter is 
bathed all in a particularly Christic atmosphere. Even such a passage 
controversial as 3:18-22, the exact meaning of which remains a matter of controversy. 
discussion among exegetes of our days, has as its protagonist 
undoubted Christ the Lord and points out his greatness. 
 Although the text of the epistle does not provide us, as is usual 
in the biblical and New Testament writings in particular, specific dates, their 
content seems to point to the years of Nero Caesar's empire, and more 
specifically at delicate moments for the Christians of Asia Minor to the 
which the epistle is addressed. It is very evident that these communities live a 
atmosphere of tension in which persecution seems to be already a reality or is going to 
take place imminently (4:12-19). Only in this way do we understand the 
exhortations to a dignified life, no longer as Christians who follow the example of 
Jesus or prominent figures of the Old Testament, but also as 
citizens of a state that could be hostile. Now this fear of harm 
that civil authorities can cause cannot generate an attitude of 
revolt or dissent against Roman power, but, on the contrary, 
insists on the need to live according to state laws (ch. 1-2). 
 The Christian, and this is, possibly, one of the greatest contributions of 
the epistle to the theology of the universal Church, must conceive itself as 
priest, that is, a member of a priestly people (2:9-10) whose function 

164

basic consists of intercession for others. Where ancient Israel 
failed, the Church of Christ must carry out this task.  
 All these characteristics make the Epistle 1 Saint Peter a writing 
capital of the New Testament, genuine representative of what has been given in 
call “primitive Catholicism”, and bearer of a message that is still today 
fundamental for the whole of Christianity and its witness in the world.

Contrary to the Epistle 1 Saint Peter, this writing had problems 
to be accepted into the New Testament canon. In fact, 
It was not until the end of Antiquity, when it was included 
among the apostolic writings, considering that it was also a work 
of the Prince of the Apostles (1:1), although not without arduous 
discussions, due to the very obvious differences in style and content with 
the previous letter. 
 The exegesis of our days has no problem in including this 
epistle in the New Testament canon, although it is classified as 
“deuteropetrina”, that is, the work of a disciple of the school of the Apostle Saint 
Peter who would have lived at the very end of the Apostolic Era itself. 
In fact, today it is considered a settled matter to believe that it is the most 
recent of the New Testament and the whole of the canonical Bible: I would have seen 
the light towards the beginning of the second decade of the second century. 
 Although at times the author follows the literary fiction of 
his days and seems to express himself as if he were the Apostle himself (1:14-18), in which 
There is evidence, without a doubt, of an undeniably Petrine tradition perpetuated among 
the disciples of the Great Fisherman of Galilee, it is very evident that the hand that 
composes the letter is another, later in time, if the tradition that 
places the end of San Pedro around the years 64 or 67 AD. C. in Nero's Rome 
Caesar. The epistle comes to describe a tense atmosphere within the 
Christian communities (chap. 2), with false teachers who destroy the 
truth received. Certain details, such as the allusions made by these dissidents 
to the heavenly powers (2:10), their lives manifestly depraved (2:13-14) 
or his alleged proclamations of freedom (2:19), would seem to point to the sects 
Gnostics that did so much damage to the Church since the end of the first century, since 
They offered an interpretation of the Christian message opposed to the teaching 
apostolic tradition and the most venerable traditions preserved in the communities 
primitive, by proclaiming a double standard that served the interests of those who, 
as an intellectually superior class, they were truly free and speculated 
over the heavenly world. If we add to it the eschatological concern that 
shows chap. 3, especially v. 9, in which we read a consciousness of 
delay of the Lord not exempt from disappointment, and the very important detail that 
The Pauline writings are already comparable with the rest of the Scriptures received from 
Israel and are studied closely because of their internal difficulties (3:15-16), 
we have a fairly complete picture of a Christian Church that has 

166

survived the death of the Apostles and is now a set of communities 
cohesive organizations faced with new and arduous challenges, only surmountable 
appealing to the teachings received about Christ and his message. 
 2 Saint Peter is a writing accessible to today's reader. His expression and his 
style is that of Hellenism at the time in which it was born, and its content, 
Despite the space-time distance, it continues to have the same relevance. The 
challenges that were presented to Christianity at that time were, mutatis 
mutandis, the same ones that the universal Church of Christ has today. Hence it is 
present as an epistle of hope in the Lord who comes soon to collect 
to his people.

According to certain very ancient traditions, Saint John the Apostle was the last of 
the Twelve to die, and he did so, apparently, after being miraculously 
rejuvenated in the persecution of Emperor Domitian. In this way, 
It is said that he reached a ripe old age as bishop of Ephesus and Asia Minor, 
loved and respected by the Christian communities of the area, who saw in him the 
last of Christ's witnesses. Such traditions have allowed us to attribute this 
epistle and the two that follow in the canonical order to Saint John the Apostle, since his 
style and its vocabulary are very close to those of the Fourth Gospel, so much so that 
It has been thought that 1 Saint John would have been conceived almost as a 
prologue or an introductory preface to that. 
 The truth is that there is nothing in the epistle itself that allows such 
affirmations. What we can objectively deduce from its content is that 
It is a very well prepared writing, with a very pastoral style, very 
close to his readers (cf. the treatment of little children that we read throughout chapter. 
2 or in 5:21, among other passages) and very loose at times, so that the 
Topics discussed do not always seem to obey a previous logical plan. This 
impression of improvisation and the concern that permeates its chapters and 
verses make this epistle a pleasant text, easy to read in our 
days and that conveys a beautiful teaching. 
 The writer expresses himself, despite his evident humility, with sufficient 
authority to be not only listened to, but also obeyed. Raise the 
Christian life as a total consecration to Christ, who is our Advocate 
(2:1-5), but above all the Word of Life, the Logos of Jn. 1:1-18. 
Likewise, this epistle proclaims the universal Christian truth that God is 
love (4:8), which, together with the statements of Jesus collected in Jn. 
3:16; 13:34; 15:12 and 15:17 has made the apostle Saint John the Apostle of Love in 
the universal Christian tradition. Hence in this letter the existence of the 
believers must be marked and marked by the reality of love. The Christian 
It is one who loves his brothers and others. In this way, it achieves this 
written a high summit of spirituality that will influence all mysticism 
later Christianity and will give its special patina to the Eastern Orthodox world. 
 But it also echoes a pressing concern, the coming of the 
Antichrist, a character that later Christian tradition will color with traits 
demonic and will make him a true myth. 2:18ff. and 4:1-3 mention 
directly to this character as someone (or something) real, already present in that 
same moment, and as evidence that the Church lives in the last 

168

time. Once again, the features with which the figure and the 
teachings of the Antichrist point to the gnostic and doctrinal currents of 
late 1st century and early 2nd century AD. C., which agrees with the 
tradition that claims to have been Saint John the Apostle, the last of the disciples of 
Jesus in dying. Likewise, they imply that these manifestations of 
Doctrinal deviation has its genesis in the Christian communities themselves. 
 Hence, 1 Saint John is not only a writing of great depth 
theological and refined spirituality, but a witness of immense value for what 
which has been called “the dark age of Christian antiquity”, is worth 
that is, the last decades of the first century, in which the Church had to fight to 
preserve your identity and integrity in the face of civil harassment by officials 
Roman imperial forces and the appearance of philosophies adverse to the gospel in their 
same breast.

As is evident from the first verse, this epistle seems to have 
some individual recipients, “the chosen lady and her children.” Despite 
to this, canonical tradition has placed it among the epistles
